hook_clip: Here's how to reverse engineer Lattice from a written spec. Claude passed all seventeen checks, and found sixty-four gaps in my spec.
outro_clip: The full spec is free at personal software factory dot com. If you build it, tell me what broke. I'm Sam. See you tomorrow.

scenes.text: We gave Claude one Markdown file. It copies the part of Lattice a small team uses for reviews. Review cycles with a question template and one to five ratings. Self reviews. Peer feedback that the employee proposes and the manager approves. And manager reviews, calibration and release on a set date.

The core rule is who sees what. The manager sees the self review once it's submitted, and peer feedback with names. The employee sees the manager's review and final rating only after release. Peer feedback reaches them without names, and only if at least two peers answered. Calibration notes, never. And a skip-level manager sees nothing at all.

Claude built it in four phases, one prompt each. The foundation and self reviews. Peer feedback. Manager reviews, calibration and release. Then reminders, history and export. After every phase, the acceptance checks ran in a real browser.

Here's what it built. The cycle dashboard shows seven reviews and each step's status. Marcus sees Kai's peer feedback on Ivy's review, with Kai's name. On Monday at nine, the reminder job sent four self review reminders. In calibration, Leo's rating moves from four to three, with a written reason. After release, Leo sees a final rating of three, and nothing about calibration. And on a phone, Kai's peer feedback page shows only the two peer questions.
In one final run, on a fresh database, all seventeen checks passed, along with one hundred and twenty-two automated tests.

But the more useful result is what broke. The test build exposed sixty-four places where Claude had to guess. Nothing stopped an admin from calibrating her own review. The spec showed the employee the overall rating, which is the rating before calibration. And one to three peers didn't say per proposal or in total. Every gap is now fixed in the spec.

Passing every check isn't the same as production-ready. We didn't test production sign-in, real email delivery, a hosted scheduler, or hosting. And no check reached a release with two peer answers, so the nameless view is covered only by unit tests.

So is it worth building? Lattice Performance is ten dollars per seat per month, billed yearly, with a four thousand dollar minimum. A team of thirty would pay three thousand six hundred dollars, so the minimum applies, up to thirty-three people. If you want one-on-ones, goals, engagement and compensation in one product, buy it. If you run one or two review cycles a year and want rules you can read, build it.
Everything is in one file. The data model, ten rules, seed data, four phase prompts, and all seventeen checks, with the sixty-four fixes already in.
